summary: Defines a BGP encoding that distributes traffic flow specifications, which describe a class of traffic by matching on packet fields, for IPv4. Routers can use these rules to filter or rate-limit matching traffic, which is useful for quickly pushing out defenses against attacks. It covers both intra-domain and inter-domain use.

eli5.summary: Network operators can broadcast a rule like drop anything that looks like this, and all their routers learn it quickly, rather than configuring each by hand.

questions: how to distribute ddos filter rules with bgp
how to drop ddos traffic with bgp
subtitle: How BGP carries traffic filter rules, so routers can drop, rate-limit, redirect or re-mark matching packets across networks.

tldr.problem: Traffic filtering policies were traditionally static, which makes it hard to react to denial-of-service attacks or coordinate filtering between providers.
tldr.mechanism: A new BGP NLRI type encodes a Flow Specification, a set of packet-header match components such as prefixes, ports and protocol. Extended Communities attached to it say what to do with matching traffic, and a validation step ties each rule to the unicast routing table.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8955 obsoletes RFC 5575 and RFC 7674 and has itself been updated by later RFCs. It adds a packet-rate action, defines all actions as transitive and adds error handling.

today: RFC 8955 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5575 and RFC 7674. It has been updated by RFC 8956, RFC 9117 and RFC 9184.

sections.title: Filter Rules Carried in BGP
sections.content:
Modern routers can classify, shape, rate limit, filter or redirect packets based on administratively defined policies. The n-tuple of matching criteria, such as source and destination prefixes, IP protocol and port numbers, is called a Flow Specification. A packet matches only if it matches all the specified criteria.

This RFC defines how to encode Flow Specifications as a BGP NLRI (Network Layer Reachability Information) for IPv4 unicast and IPv4 BGP/MPLS VPN services. It also defines BGP Extended Communities that carry the Traffic Filtering Actions to apply to matching packets. The aim is to distribute filtering rules within and between providers, for example to mitigate DoS and DDoS attacks.

Using BGP lets a provider reuse its route distribution infrastructure (such as route reflectors) and its existing inter-domain BGP sessions with customers. The RFC notes the information can be originated manually or by systems that detect malicious flows, and that automated systems need care. IPv6 is handled in RFC 8956.
sections.eli5: Instead of walking to every router to type in a rule, an operator tells one router, and the news spreads along the same channels routers already use to share maps.

sections.title: The Flow Specification NLRI
sections.content:
Flow Specifications use the BGP multiprotocol attributes MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI. Peers must advertise the Multiprotocol Extension Capability with AFI 1 and SAFI 133 for IPv4 Flow Specification, or SAFI 134 for VPNv4 Flow Specification. The Next-Hop length MUST be 0 and its address is ignored.

Each NLRI starts with a length of one octet, or two octets when the length is 240 or more (the top nibble is then 0xf). The highest value this can represent is 4095. The NLRI value is a list of components in strictly increasing type order, each type at most once, and a packet must match the intersection (AND) of all components present. An NLRI that is not encoded as specified, including one with an unknown component type, is malformed.

For the VPN family, the NLRI is an 8-octet Route Distinguisher followed by the same NLRI value, and propagation is controlled by Route Target matching with the VRF import policy.
sections.eli5: A rule is written as a checklist in a fixed order, like name, then grade, then class. A packet only counts as a match if it ticks every box on the list.

sections.title: Components and Operators
sections.content:
Each component begins with a one-octet type. The IPv4 types are Destination Prefix (1), Source Prefix (2), IP Protocol (3), Port (4), Destination Port (5), Source Port (6), ICMP Type (7), ICMP Code (8), TCP Flags (9), Packet Length (10), DSCP (11) and Fragment (12).

Most components hold a list of operator and value pairs. The numeric operator has an end-of-list bit, an AND bit (unset means OR with the previous pair, and AND binds tighter than OR), a length field for 1, 2, 4 or 8 octets, and lt, gt and eq bits that combine into comparisons such as less-or-equal and not-equal. The bitmask operator replaces the comparison bits with a NOT bit and a match bit, used for TCP Flags and Fragment.

Some components can never match certain traffic. Port components never match packets whose IP protocol is not TCP (6) or UDP (17), non-first fragments, or packets whose transport header the system cannot locate. ICMP components work similarly for protocol 1. Combinations that can never match, such as ICMP Type AND Port, SHOULD NOT be propagated.

The RFC gives worked encodings. For example, "all packets to 192.0.2.0/24 and TCP port 25" is an 11-octet NLRI.
sections.eli5: Each box on the checklist can say things like "bigger than 10" or "exactly 25". The operator is just the little word that tells how to compare.

sections.title: Ordering and Validation
sections.content:
More than one Flow Specification may match a flow, so the order must not depend on arrival order. The comparison starts at the lowest component type. A rule with a lower-numbered component type before the other has precedence. For prefixes, the more specific prefix wins, and otherwise the lower IP value wins. Other components are compared as binary strings with memcmp(), where the lowest string wins, and for a common prefix the longer string takes precedence. Appendix A gives Python code.

A rule received from an external peer is only accepted if it is validated against unicast routing. By default it is feasible only if all of these hold:

  • It contains a destination prefix component.
  • Its originator matches the originator of the best-match unicast route for that prefix.
  • No more-specific unicast route comes from a different neighboring AS than that best match.

Rule one MAY be relaxed by explicit configuration. Implementations MUST also require the neighboring AS in the left-most position of the AS_PATH on eBGP routes, and MUST revalidate whenever unicast routes change. The idea is that the AS advertising the best unicast route for a destination may ask for traffic to it to be dropped, since that is as if it were dropped downstream. Rules received via SAFI 133 are checked against SAFI 1 routes and rules via SAFI 134 against SAFI 128.
sections.eli5: If two rules apply, there is a fair way to pick which goes first. And you only believe a rule about a street if it comes from the person who actually owns that street.

sections.title: Traffic Filtering Actions
sections.content:
Actions are carried as transitive BGP Extended Communities. The default action for a matching rule is to accept the packet with normal forwarding. Several actions may be present for one rule and SHOULD all be applied. If they cannot be, they interfere, and it is an implementation decision which are used, which implementors SHOULD document.

  • traffic-rate-bytes (0x8006) and traffic-rate-packets (0x800c): a maximum rate as an IEEE floating point number, in bytes or packets per second. A rate of 0 discards all traffic for the flow.
  • traffic-action (0x8007): two defined bits. Terminal Action (bit 47) says whether later rules are still evaluated, and Sample (bit 46) enables sampling and logging.
  • rt-redirect (0x8008, 0x8108, 0x8208): redirects traffic to a VRF that imports the given route target.
  • traffic-marking (0x8009): rewrites the DSCP bits to the encoded value.

Implementations SHOULD also provide a way to log packet headers of filtered traffic and to count matches for each rule.
sections.eli5: Once a packet matches, the rule says what to do: let it through slowly, throw it away, send it down a different hallway, or stick a new label on it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As long as Flow Specifications are restricted to match unicast routing paths (the validation above), the security characteristics are equivalent to those of BGP unicast routing. Relaxing validation can let unwanted rules spread, causing unwanted filtering, re-marking or redirection. Networks that relax it need extra BGP policy filtering, and specifications that relax it MUST describe the required filtering.

Other risks the RFC lists:

  • At Internet Exchange Points, route servers often do not extend the AS_PATH, so the left-most AS check cannot be enforced. A strict inbound route policy is advised.
  • Misprogrammed controllers or rogue systems may announce unintended rules or send them at a high rate, stressing receivers.
  • Non-traffic-rate actions let a third party change forwarding, even reaching other VPNs or queues. Operators should filter these at borders, for example by mapping user-defined communities to actions.
  • Routers have limited capacity, so providers may need to cap the number of rules accepted.
sections.eli5: A powerful announcement system is only safe if you check who is allowed to speak. Otherwise a troublemaker could tell everybody to stop the wrong people.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 5575
sections.content:
RFC 8955 obsoletes RFC 5575 and also RFC 7674, whose redirect clarification it folds into Section 7.4. The authors point out these technical changes:

  • The NLRI is no longer treated as an opaque key, and the meaning of the numeric comparison bit combinations is defined.
  • The allowed value lengths for components are stated consistently.
  • All action communities are defined as transitive. RFC 5575 made traffic-rate non-transitive and said nothing about the others.
  • A new traffic-rate-packets action is added, and the redirect actions are renamed rt-redirect.
  • Guidance on interfering actions and a new error handling section were added. Error handling follows RFC 7606 and RFC 4760.
sections.eli5: This is the new edition of the rulebook. It fixes unclear spots and adds a new kind of speed limit.

items.desc: Match source or destination TCP/UDP port.

data.title: All packets to 192.0.2.0/24 and TCP port 25
data.code:
length | destination    | protocol | port
0x0b   | 01 18 c0 00 02 | 03 81 06 | 04 81 19

0x0b length = 11 octets
01 = Type 1 Destination Prefix, 18 = 24 bits, c0 00 02 = 192.0.2
03 = Type 3 IP Protocol, 81 = end-of-list, size 1, ==, 06 = TCP
04 = Type 4 Port, 81 = end-of-list, size 1, ==, 19 = 25
